title: Basic Sheep and Goat Anatomy and Abnormalities;

lessons.title: The outside of the carcass: muscles, bones and lymph nodes
lessons.html:
Why a slaughterer needs anatomy

When you know where the organs, bones and joints of a sheep or goat are, you can dress the carcass faster, cut in the right places, avoid cutting the guts, and recognise when something looks wrong.

The skeleton and joints

  • Head is removed at the joint between the skull and the first neck bone (the atlas joint).
  • Front feet are removed at the knee joint (carpal joint).
  • Hind feet are removed at the hock joint (tarsal joint).
  • Spine: neck, back, loin and tail bones.
  • Breastbone (sternum): in front of the chest. It is opened or split during evisceration in some plants.
  • Pelvis (aitch bone): at the back; the rectum and bladder pass through here.

Main cuts and muscle areas

On a lamb carcass the main parts are the neck, shoulder, rib (rack), loin, leg and breast. Valuable cuts like the leg and loin must not be damaged with knife cuts.

Lymph nodes

Lymph nodes are small bean-shaped glands found in the fat and between muscles. They filter germs. When an animal is sick, the lymph nodes near the problem often become swollen. The meat inspector cuts and looks at certain lymph nodes. Do not cut or remove lymph nodes; the meat inspector needs to see them.

Fat

A good carcass has an even cover of white or cream fat. The fat protects the meat while it chills. Do not tear the fat during skinning.

lessons.title: The organs inside
lessons.html:
The chest (thorax)

  • Heart: a firm muscle in the middle of the chest, with fat at the top.
  • Lungs: pink and spongy, on both sides of the heart.
  • Windpipe (trachea): from the throat to the lungs.

The belly (abdomen)

  • Liver: large, dark red-brown, on the right side just behind the diaphragm. The gall bladder is attached to it.
  • Stomach: sheep and goats are ruminants and have four stomach compartments: rumen (the big one), reticulum, omasum and abomasum. The rumen is full of chewed grass and fluid.
  • Intestines: small and large intestines, ending at the rectum.
  • Kidneys: two, bean-shaped, under the loin, covered in fat.
  • Spleen: flat, purple-grey, attached to the rumen.
  • Bladder: in the pelvis.

The diaphragm (skirt) is a thin muscle wall that separates the chest from the belly.

Red offal and rough offal

Red offalRough offal
Heart, lungs, liver, kidneys, tongue, spleenStomachs (tripe), intestines

The rumen and intestines contain dung and germs. If they are cut during evisceration, the carcass is contaminated. Know where they lie, so you can open the belly safely.

lessons.title: Recognising abnormalities
lessons.html:
Normal and abnormal

Only the meat inspector decides if meat is fit to eat. But slaughterers see every carcass closely. If you see something unusual, you must tell the meat inspector and not cut it out or hide it.

Abnormalities you may see

What you seePossible cause
Bruises: dark red or purple areas in the meatRough handling or transport injury
Abscess: a lump full of pusInfection, for example from a wound or injection
Small fluid-filled bubbles (cysts) in the liver, lungs or meatTapeworm cysts (measles, hydatid cysts)
Liver with thick, hard white bile ducts or flat leaf-shaped wormsLiver fluke
Lungs that are dark, firm or stuck to the chest wallPneumonia
Swollen lymph nodes, yellow fat or meat, a bad smellDisease, jaundice or infection
Very thin carcass with watery, jelly-like fatPoor condition or long illness

What to do

  1. Do not cut into the abnormal area.
  2. Keep the carcass, head and organs together.
  3. Call the meat inspector.
  4. Follow the inspector's decision.
  5. Sterilise your knife if it touched pus or diseased tissue.

Some diseases can spread to people. Wash your hands well and cover any cuts.

Key points

  • Knowing anatomy helps you cut in the right place and avoid gut cuts.
  • Sheep and goats are ruminants with four stomach compartments.
  • Red offal: heart, lungs, liver, kidneys; rough offal: stomachs and intestines.
  • Do not cut or remove lymph nodes; the inspector needs them.
  • Report bruises, abscesses, cysts and other abnormalities to the meat inspector.
